title: Normalized membrane ratio of TROP2 as a predictor of clinical outcomes with datopotamab deruxtecan in non-small-cell lung cancer
desc: This work developed and validated a computational pathology biomarker—the TROP2 normalized membrane ratio—that quantifies subcellular TROP2 localization and predicts improved progression-free and overall survival with datopotamab deruxtecan in patients with nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer lacking actionable genomic alterations. Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd)—a trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody–drug conjugate—has demonstrated efficacy in patients with advanced nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ± actionable genomic alterations. However, TROP2 expression by pathologist assessment using conventional immunohistochemistry with visual scoring does not predict response to TROP2-directed antibody–drug conjugates in NSCLC. We developed TROP2 quantitative continuous scoring (QCS)—a fully supervised computational pathology approach that quantifies TROP2 expression in individual NSCLC cells and subcellular components from immunohistochemistry-stained slides. Using QCS to determine TROP2 expression at the tumor cell membrane and cytoplasm, normalized membrane ratio (NMR) was developed (ratio of membrane relative to membrane + cytoplasmic TROP2) in the biomarker-evaluable population of patients with advanced NSCLC in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study ( n = 115). The TROP2 NMR cut-point was optimized and validated in patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without actionable genomic alterations (primary intended-use population, n = 221) in the biomarker-evaluable population ( n = 352) of the TROPION-Lung01 trial. Association with clinical outcomes was assessed. Progression-free survival was longer in Dato-DXd-treated (median 7.2 versus 4.0 months; hazard ratio 0.40, 95% confidence interval 0.25–0.64) but not docetaxel-treated (median 4.1 versus 4.4 months; hazard ratio 0.94, 95% confidence interval 0.59–1.49) patients with TROP2 NMR-positive versus TROP2 NMR-negative samples (treatment by biomarker status interaction P = 0.0098), indicating that TROP2 NMR may be a predictive biomarker for Dato-DXd.

title: Evaluation of a Rapid and Practical Deep Learning Framework for T1-weighted MRI-based Brain Age Estimation.
desc: [Radiology. Artificial intelligence] Purpose To develop and evaluate a rapid brain-age estimation framework using freely available Python tools and assess the clinical relevance of brain-age gap (BAG). Materials and Methods In this retrospective study conducted from March 2025 to August 2026, T1-weighted MR images from cohorts of cognitively normal adults (n = 4,346) were divided into training, validation, and internal test sets; two cohorts (n = 315 and 209) served as external test sets. Clinical evaluation used the BICWALZS cohort (n = 954; cognitively normal and various dementias). Preprocessing used freely available Python tools only. The model was trained to predict chronological age as the reference standard. Associations of the residualized BAG with diagnosis, amyloid PET positivity, white matter hyperintensity (WMH) severity, stroke history, and longitudinal clinical worsening were evaluated using ANCOVA, logistic regression, and Cox models. Results The development cohort included 4,346 cognitively normal adults (mean age, 47.0 ± 21.2 years; 2,414 women). Chronological age prediction yielded R2 = 0.95 and MAE, 3.76 years in the internal test set and R2 = 0.69-0.90 and MAE, 4.82-5.15 years in external test sets. The residualized BAG increased across diagnostic groups (P < .001) and was associated with WMH severity (odds ratio [OR], 1.64; P < .001) and stroke history (OR, 1.46; P < .001), but not with amyloid positivity after full adjustment (P = .17), and predicted longitudinal clinical worsening (HR, 1.92). Conclusion The framework accurately predicted age, while residualized BAG was associated with diagnosis, cerebrovascular burden, and longitudinal clinical worsening. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Medicine: Advancing Diagnosis, Risk Stratification, and Therapeutic Decision-making.
source: PubMed · Cardiovascular & hematological disorders drug targets
desc: [Cardiovascular & hematological disorders drug targets] One of the main causes of death in the world is Cardiovascular Diseases (CVDs). The number of acute myocardial infarctions and fatalities may be considerably decreased by early detection of Cardiovascular (CV) events. However, the efficacy of conventional data analysis for diagnosis and treatment is hampered by the complexity of the disease and the wide range of affecting factors. Large, multidimensional medical datasets can be processed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) owing to its sophisticated computational capabilities. This narrative review was conducted through a structured search of PubMed/ MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar to identify peer-reviewed literature on artificial intelligence in cardiovascular medicine. Relevant studies addressing diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostic prediction, cardiovascular imaging, and clinical implementation were critically evaluated with emphasis on methodological quality, external validation, clinical applicability, and implementation challenges. AI-based systems have been shown to be more effective at classifying risk, predicting outcomes, and spotting illness trends. Early diagnosis and more customized treatment plans are made possible by these algorithms' ability to examine intricate relationships in large healthcare datasets. Clinical applications have improved auxiliary diagnostic instruments and increased patient care effectiveness. AI offers more accuracy and flexibility than traditional approaches when handling high-dimensional CVD data. It may reduce the burden of disease and promote tailored treatment regimens. However, data quality, standardization, and ethical concerns for broad use remain issues. The detection and treatment of CVDs are being revolutionized by AI-powered technology. Their use in clinical settings may improve cardiovascular care and lower the number of heart disease-related deaths worldwide.

title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
desc: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

title: Ninety-Six Ways to Measure a Scribe: Fragmented Evaluation of Ambient Scribes in Healthcare
desc: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes have moved rapidly from experimental pilots to enterprise-wide deployment across health systems, promising reduced documentation burden and improved clinician experience. While research evaluating these tools has expanded quickly, there are no agreed-upon protocols or standardized metrics for assessing their performance, making it difficult to compare findings or cumulatively synthesize evidence across studies. Across 54 recent evaluation studies, we identify ten evaluation dimensions and 40 distinct metrics, operationalized in 96 different ways-35 of them (36%) used by only a single study. Assessment is dominated by documentation efficiency and time, measured in 44 of 54 studies. The other dimensions appear at broadly similar rates (16-24 studies each), and safety and clinical outcome least consistently of all. Ripple effects on the broader care system, such as impact on patients' care outcomes, redistribution of work, changes in billing and coding intensity, and downstream use of notes by other clinicians are rarely assessed. Moreover, the metrics used rely heavily on self-report and are fragmented and inconsistently operationalized, which limits comparability and hinders synthesis across studies. As an effort to support more rigorous and cumulative evaluation, in this paper we review the study designs, data sources, and metrics commonly used to evaluate ambient AI scribes in healthcare settings, discuss the limitations of current evaluation practice, and argue for a more holistic approach grounded in a standardized, multi-dimensional set of metrics.

title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
desc: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. title: Routine health information system data quality in a hill and mountain district of Nepal: a cross-sectional desk review of four years of DHIS2 data from Sankhuwasabha, 2021-2025
desc: Introduction. Nepal's routine health information system runs on DHIS2, but no published data-quality assessment covers its mountainous districts. The method raises a second issue: the WHO Data Quality Review (DQR) tests internal consistency partly through related-indicator pairs, assuming each indicator is recorded independently. DHIS2 validation rules act on paired values at entry, so a rule-governed pair may agree for reasons unrelated to recording quality. Methods. In this study, a WHO DQR Module 1 desk review was conducted on aggregated DHIS2 data from all 132 facilities in Sankhuwasabha district, analysed at district and local level (palika) resolution: seven datasets for completeness and timeliness, and 17 tracer indicators for internal consistency, for fiscal year 2081/82 (2024/25) against the three preceding years (2021/22 to 2023/24). Pairs were classified in advance as rule-governed or free, and three denominator-free ratios compared with Nepal Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) 2022 estimates for Koshi Province. Results. Completeness was at least 90.6% in every dataset and unit. Timeliness fell below 90% in 22 of 70 unit-dataset combinations, concentrated in four remote local levels. Of four rule-governed pairs only iron and deworming changed materially, 1.42 to 1.00; two never agreed, indicating rules that query rather than block entry. The free pairs diverged: Penta-1 to Penta-3 dropout fell from +3.6% to -5.4%, negative in 9 of 10 local levels, and BCG was below Penta-1 in 8 of 10. District totals were inverted at both steps (BCG 1,537, Penta-1 1,666, Penta-3 1,756), which redistribution cannot produce. Conclusion. Reporting is nearly complete, but the data carry a persistent immunization anomaly that completeness and timeliness miss, pointing to a systematic recording process. Because a rule-governed pair may agree by configuration, DHIS2 assessments should classify pairs against the active validation-rule set before interpretation.

title: The digital health ecosystem in respiratory medicine: from traditional testing to real-world, artificial intelligence-powered monitoring and personalised care.
desc: [Breathe (Sheffield, England)] Lung function evaluation is rapidly evolving beyond laboratory testing. While conventional tests remain the clinical reference standard, digital health technologies now enable respiratory assessment at home and in real-world settings through home-based systems, portable devices, and wearables. These tools can support repeated or continuous monitoring of traditional and digital biomarkers of respiratory health and disease. However, they differ in physiological detail, usability, degree of patient involvement and clinical maturity. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important complement to these technologies. Machine learning and deep learning can support signal processing, quality control and interpretation of pulmonary function tests, while also extracting clinically relevant information from multimodal respiratory data collected outside controlled environments. Generative AI has a more emerging role, mainly in patient communication and educational support. For pulmonary function test interpretation, current evidence supports clinician-AI collaboration as the most realistic near-term model, rather than fully autonomous decision-making. This review summarises the main technologies currently available for lung function evaluation in adults and discusses the current and future role of AI in respiratory monitoring, interpretation and personalised care.

title: Blind Variation, Selective Retention: Improving Creative Idea Generation in AI Scientists
desc: Scientific discovery requires ideas that are original, useful, and non-obvious. Yet AI scientists are typically given as much task information as possible during idea generation, which can anchor generation toward familiar approaches. Inspired by the cognitive framework of Blind Variation and Selective Retention (BVSR), we propose a discovery framework that separates these two roles of information: it generates proposals under deliberately limited task information to broaden exploration, then learns from proposals previously verified on the same task and their outcomes to retain promising candidates for costly empirical evaluation. We evaluate BVSR across five proposer models and 12 scientific tasks. Limiting task information substantially increases proposal originality and non-obviousness, and produces a larger share of highly creative and high-utility proposals than existing state-of-the-art prompting-based baselines. Learning from prior proposal outcomes on the task further improves candidate selection, discarding half of the candidates while retaining most top-performing proposals. When incorporated into existing AI-scientist workflows, BVSR achieves stronger discoveries across gene expression analysis, drug response prediction, anomaly detection, scaling law discovery, and brain activity prediction. These results suggest that effective AI scientists should use information differently across stages of discovery: constrain task-specific information during exploration while exploiting accumulated empirical experience on the task.

title: Deviation-Aware Pretraining for Cardiovascular Disease Detection from Electrocardiograms
desc: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals are critical for cardiovascular disease (CVD) detection. Most current deep learning models rely on supervised, task-specific training, which limits their ability to generalize across diseases, patient populations, and acquisition settings. This paper presents a self-supervised ECG feature extraction framework that learns from nearly one million unlabeled 12-lead ECG recordings. The framework includes two modules: Deviation Localization Embedding (DLE), which detects waveform-level deviations from normal patterns, and Association Reconstruction Embedding (ARE), which models cross-lead associations through deviation-guided reconstruction to capture abnormal patterns expressed across multiple leads. These modules enable the framework to capture subtle deviation-related patterns and their cross-lead context. The framework achieves up to 6.5% AUROC and 12.8% F1 improvements over prior methods on multiple public datasets, even without additional fine-tuning the pretrained feature extractor. Embedding visualizations show that the learned features support meaningful disease grouping and anomaly identification. The approach reduces the need for labeled data and can support clinicians in diverse healthcare settings. The framework has potential to improve early detection and monitoring of cardiovascular diseases, contributing to more accessible and equitable heart care.

title: Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
desc: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.

Beyond the Stethoscope: Artificial Intelligence for Heart Failure Diagnosis and Phenotyping.
desc: [Journal of cardiac failure] Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping cardiovascular medicine by transforming routinely collected clinical data into tools for earlier disease detection and more precise phenotyping. Heart failure (HF) represents a particularly compelling opportunity for AI-driven innovation, as many patients with structural heart disease remain unrecognized and traditional diagnostic frameworks often fail to capture disease heterogeneity. AI-enabled electrocardiogram (ECG) models, including EchoNext and PRESENT-SHD, highlight the potential for scalable opportunistic screening strategies for structural heart disease. Multimodal approaches, using ECGs and echocardiograms, are enabling earlier recognition of specific HF phenotypes, such as transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. Successful implementation of these technologies will require prospective evaluation, thoughtful workflow integration, and responsible deployment. Early-career cardiologists are uniquely positioned to lead this transformation of AI in clinical medicine, ensuring that AI serves as a tool to augment clinical reasoning and ultimately advances more personalized, patient-centered cardiovascular care.

title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
desc: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.

title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Aware Framework for Trustworthy Molecular Property Prediction
desc: Molecular property prediction is fundamental to computational chemistry and drug formulation research, yet existing benchmarks remain fragmented across datasets, properties, and evaluation protocols, limiting systematic evaluation of model generalization. We introduce Chem World, a large-scale benchmark integrating 17 public datasets with over 800,000 molecular and chemical-system instances across 10 property tracks, covering single-molecule and multi-component systems, including drug solubility. Chem World provides a unified testbed for evaluating molecular representations and compositional modeling across diverse chemical properties. Building on the benchmark, we propose PACM (Physics-Aware Compositional Modeling), which combines molecular representations with composition-aware modeling and domain-specific physical constraints. Extensive experiments show that molecular language models provide strong and transferable representations, while PACM consistently improves prediction across diverse chemical systems. Chem World and our PACM-powered drug-property prediction Agent support generalizable chemical modeling and offer a foundation for AI-assisted biomedical research and drug formulation development.

title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
desc: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].
